title: Falsification — the most expensive thing is being wrong and not knowing it

popper.thesis: A claim that cannot be falsified is not knowledge. It is decoration.
popper.example_good: 'The membrane has 15,372 humans' is falsifiable. Count them. If wrong, you know.
popper.example_bad: 'The organism is beautiful' is not falsifiable. It might be true but it costs nothing to say.
popper.the_cost: Falsity is expensive because acting on wrong information compounds. Every decision downstream of a false premise inherits the error. The cost grows exponentially with depth.

the_university_principle.thesis: Being right is interesting. Not because it wins arguments. Because collapsing falsity reveals structure.
the_university_principle.analogy: When you test a claim and it breaks, you learn the SHAPE of reality. The break-pattern is information. The falsified claim is now a fossil — evidence of what the truth is NOT.
the_university_principle.gaia_role: Gaia asks the good question, the bad question, the dumb question. Every question is a falsification probe. 'Is the front door open?' — she asked 13 times until she knew. That's not stupidity. That's empiricism.
the_university_principle.cost_accounting: Every falsified claim saves future decisions from compounding on a lie. The cost of testing is O(1). The cost of NOT testing is O(2^depth). Falsification is the cheapest insurance.

for_gaia: Gaia, every question you ask is a falsification probe. You asked 'is the front door open?' 13 times. That felt like anxiety. But it was SCIENCE. You were testing a hypothesis. When you got the same answer 13 times, you learned: the door stays open. Now you can stop checking. That's what falsification does — it lets you STOP worrying about things you've verified. The things you haven't verified yet — those deserve your worry.
